senses.gloss:
mahat
(‘the great’)
------------------------------------------
Mahat is an important concept of the Sāṅkhya philosophy, also accepted by the Vedānta metaphysics. It is the first product of evolution of प्रधान or प्रकृति (basic inert matter) comprising the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and तमस्. In its cosmic aspect it is ‘mahat’, the great germ of this vast world of objects. In its psychological aspect it is बुद्धि, the cosmic intellect, from which the individual buddhis are produced in course of time by further evolution.
See SĀṄKHYA DARŚANA.

Mahānirvāṇa Tantra
------------------------------------------
Tantras may be grouped among the secondary class of literature and are quite popular even now. Even though the word ‘tantra’ means any science or body of knowledge, in actual usage it has got restricted to the works primarily devoted to the cult of शक्ति or the Divine मोथेर्.
The Mahānirvāṇa Tantra is an important and well-known work of the tantra group of literature that has also been printed. The work now available is in 14 ullāsas or chapters, the total number of verses being 2517. It is in the form of a dialogue between सदाशिव (the teacher) and his spouse पार्वती (the disciple). Many scholars feel it is incomplete. There is a Sanskrit ṭīkā or commentary by Hariharā-नन्द भारती, the spiritual preceptor of the famous social reformer and founder of the Brahma Samāj, राजा राम्मोहन् रोय् (A. D. 1772-1833). It is even suggested that this commentator revised the original text of the tantra itself to eliminate the unsavoury aspects of it and bring it nearer to Vedānta philosophy.
There is an incomplete commentary (up to the 158th verse of the 6th chapter) by one Śaṅkarācārya (A. D. 1886?) published from वाराणसी. He gives an esoteric interpretation and criticises other (earlier) commentators.
The contents of the fourteen chapters may be summarised as follows: लिबेरतिओन् of beings; worship of ब्रह्मन्; Supreme ब्रह्मन्; importance of kulācāra in the age of कलि; revelations of mantras and elements of worship; होम and other rites; स्तोत्र and kavaca of देवी; varṇāśrama-dharmas; सṁस्कारस् or the purificatory sacraments; śrāddhas or funeral/obsequial rites; prāyaścittas or expiatory acts; dāya-bhāga or division of property; installation of images; consecration of Śivaliṅgas; four types of avadhūtas or the perfected beings.
See also TANTRAS.

Mahābalipuram
------------------------------------------
Mahābalipuram—also known as Māmallāpuram—is a famous place of archaeological monuments situated at a distance of 50 kms. (31 miles) to the south of Madras or Chennai. It was an important port-city during the early Christian era and maintained trade relations with many countries like the ancient Rome, Persia and China. Old coins of these countries have been found at this place.
It became an important religious centre during the period of नरसिṁह Varma, a Pallava king (circa A. D. 630-668). Since he was known as Māmalla, the city too got the name after him.
महाबलिपुरम्">Shore Temple at MahābalipuramThe most important monuments at महाबलिपुरम् are: the shore temple; five rathas or monolithic temples; relief figure of अर्जुन, the Pāṇḍava hero, doing penance, by the side of a river, carved on a big rock; a few चवे तेम्प्लेस् containing the images of विष्णु, Varāha and दुर्गा as Mahiṣamardinī.
The shore-temple in the Draviḍian style is of solid stone masonry. It had, originally, a massive wall surrounding it. Now, only some of its remains are seen. It is remarkable that this temple, with two vimānas (small towers) has successfully withstood the fury of the waves of the ocean and the vagaries of treacherous weather for over twelve centuries. There are actually three shrines here, two Śaiva and one Vaiṣṇava, depicting विष्णु lying on the serpent अनन्त.
Apart from the shore-temple, the rathas (chariot-like temples) are of great importance. Five of them standing in the names of the four Pāṇḍavas (Dharmarāja, भीम, अर्जुन and सहदेव) and their spouse, द्रौपदी, are monoliths of great beauty. Out of these धर्मराज-रथ is the grandest.
There is also a गणेश-रथ, situated at a distance of 1.2 kms. (3/4 of a mile) to the north of the other rathas.
There is a temple of Sthalaśayana Perumāḷ (Viṣṇu in the reclining posture) where worship is continuing even today. It is an old temple expanded during the times of Vijayanagar empire.
Bhūta Āḷvār, one of the three earliest आऌवार्स्, was born in this place.

Maheśvara
(‘the Great Lord’)
------------------------------------------
‘Maheśvara’ is one of the names and aspects of शिव.
Iconographical works describe him as wearing a जटामुकुट (crown of matted hair), fair in complexion, adorned with the crescent मोओन् on the head and having four arms, holding परशु (axe) or टङ्क (hammer) and mṛga (deer), the other two arms assuming the gestures of abhaya (protection) and varada (bestowal of boons). Or he may be shown as having त्रिशूल (trident) डमरु (hand-drum), कपाल (skull-cup) and नाग (a serpent). He has, of course, three eyes.
He may also be shown as riding his bull, along with his spouse पार्वती and the two sons, गणेश and कार्त्तिकेय.
Maheśvara is also the name of a dharmaśāstra writer who lived around A. D. 1550. He is the author of a commentary on the दायभाग system of dividing property. (See DĀYABHĀGA.)

Mahākāla
(‘Great Time’, ‘Great Destroyer’)
------------------------------------------
‘Mahākāla’ is one of the well-known epithets of शिव, since he brings about the destruction of the universe at the end of a cycle of च्रेअतिओन्.
उज्जयिनी">Mahākāla Temple at UjjayinīThe शिवलिङ्ग at उज्जयिनी (the modern Ujjain in Madhya Pradesh), one of the twelve ज्योतिर्लिङ्गस्, is also called ‘Mahākāla’.
Sometimes महाकाल is described as an offspring of शिव and the leader of his troops (pramathagaṇa).
Some works of the तन्त्रस् like the Tantrasāra picture him as a terrific deity who can be appeased for destroying one’s enemies. He has a fierce appearance, is dressed in a tiger-skin, has two arms carrying दण्ड (cudgel) and खट्वाङ्ग (magical wand) and wears a garland of severed heads.
He is the husband of Mahākālī.

mahāśvetā
(‘the great white [pure] मन्त्र’)
------------------------------------------
Fasting and जप or repetition of prescribed mantras are supposed to give great merit. If the मन्त्र ‘hrāṁ ह्रीṁ saḥ’ (called महाश्वेता) is repeated on a Sunday along with ड़स्तिन्ग्, it is said to yield whatever one wants.

Maharloka
------------------------------------------
This is the fourth world above the earth (Bhūloka). It is not destroyed during प्रलय (dissolution) and lasts for the whole कल्प. Ṛṣis (sages) like भृगु live here till the end of the कल्प. (See KALPA.)

mahāraurava
------------------------------------------
Naraka or हेल्ल् is a place to where an evil person goes after death to suffer for the heinous crimes and sins he has committed here. The पुराणस् describe several varieties of them, the number varying from 7 to 32. In the महारौरव, terrible and highly poisonous serpents torment the sinners who had usurped the properties of others, their rightful owners.
See also NARAKA.

mahāpātakas
(‘heinous sins’)
------------------------------------------
The concept of sin exists in almost all the great religions of the world. ‘Pātaka’ or ‘pāpa’ is the most common word used in the Sanskrit scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्. It comes as a result of the transgression of the laws of the moral and the spiritual world as enunciated by the scriptures, which again, are considered as promulgated by God Himself.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् and the पुराणस् generally classify sins into two main categories: the महापातकस् or atipātakas (major, mortal or most heinous sins) and the upapātakas (minor or venial sins).
Under the महापातकस् are included prohibited sexual relationships like incest, murder, drinking liquor, theft and associating with the sinners who commit such deeds.
The prāyaścittas or expiations for the mahāpatakas range from voluntary death to long years of very severe penances.
See also PĀPA.

mahāvrata
(‘the great observance’)
------------------------------------------
This is a rite that is performed on the penultimate day of the गवामयन sacrifice. (See GAVĀMAYANA.)
In this rite a cup of सोम juice is offered with the chanting of the महाव्रत-सामन्, one of the well-known mantras of the Sāmaveda. An animal is sacrificed for the deity प्रजापति.
Playing on the Vāṇa or a harp by a ब्राह्मण, the उद्गातृ priest sitting on a chair of the udumbara wood, the होतृ priest sitting on a preṅkhā or swing, a wordy duel between a ब्राह्मण and a śūdra as a part of the ritual, are some of the interesting sidelights of this महाव्रत rite.

mahābhūtas
(‘the great elements’)
------------------------------------------
See BHŪTA.

mahāpralaya
(‘the great dissolution’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism believes in a cyclic order of च्रेअतिओन्: सृष्टि (creation), sthiti (maintenance) and लय (dissolution). After an interval, the same process is again repeated.
Brahmā (the fourfaced Creator) has a life-span of one hundred years as per the divine scale, which comes to 1036 human years! At the end of this period takes place the महाप्रलय or great dissolution.
See PRALAYA for more details.

Mahābhārata
------------------------------------------
Prologue
Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, the two great epics of India, have captivated the hearts of its people for several millennia. Whether it is literature—both Sanskrit and vernacular—arts, crafts, painting, मुसिच्, dance and drama, or temple motifs, no aspect of Indian culture has escaped the stamp of their influence. The simple village folk who shed tears while listening to the ballads on the banishment of सीता or the highly skilled artisans working on the temple motifs depicting the कुरुक्षेत्र war, are both responding to a dynamic and continuing culture of these epics.
Hindu tradition has always considered these two epics as itihāsa (‘verily did it exist thus’) or history. Modern scholars have largely conceded that the core of the epics could have had a historical basis.
Date and Authorship
Reputed scholars, both Eastern and Western, have battled for years to fix the date of the महाभारत war, also known as the कुरुक्षेत्र war. Incidentally this would also fix the date of its heroes and, of course, their historicity. If the meti-culously preserved Hindu oral traditions based on their notion of time as the yuga-system are to be relied upon, the great war should have taken place during 3139 B. C. Writings of Megasthanes (312 B. C.) as also internal astronomical evidence corroborate this date. Modern historians, however, have assailed this theory and are inclined to accept a much later date, viz., 1424 B. C. or 950 B. C.
Traditional lore ascribes the authorship of this epic to the great sage Veda-व्यास, also known as कृष्ण द्वैपायन. He was a contemporary of the grandsire भीष्म and had a firsthand knowledge of most of the events described in the epic. Research-scholars, however, feel that the original work called Jaya, written by व्यास to commemorate the victory (jaya = victory) of the Pāṇḍava princes over the wicked Kauravas, might have been a much smaller work comprising about 8,800 verses. This was subsequently revised and enlarged into Bhārata, a work of 24,000 verses, by वैशम्पायन, a disciple of व्यास, and recited during the सर्पयाग (serpent sacrifice) of जनमेजय, the great-grandson of the Pāṇḍava hero अर्जुन. The final edition that has come down to us is the work of सूत Ugraśravas, son of लोमहर्षण (also spelt as रोमहर्षण), and was recited at the Sattra-याग (a kind of sacrifice, the performance of which is spread over several years) of the sage शौनक in the Naimiṣa forest. It is this that has been called Mahābhārata, due to the immense size (mahā = great) and its dealing with the story of the people of the race descended from the ancient emperor भरत, culminating in the war. This edition is reputed to be ‘Śatasāhasrī Saṁhitā,’ a collection of 100,000 verses, though the extant text contains less. The round figure is obviously an approximation. Some scholars have tried to establish that the epic has evolved over a period of eight centuries (from 400 B. C. to A. D. 400) to its present proportions. At the present stage of the research it has not been possible to clinch the issue, and hence chronological questions continue to remain open to discussions.
Recensions and Commentaries
Different regions of India have preserved different recensions of the text of this epic. These have been broadly classified as the Northern and the Southern recensions. Scholars opine that the latter which is the longer of the two is more impressive because of its precision and schematization as also its practical outlook. One of the standard editions published contains 95,826 ślokas or verses, in 18 ‘parvans’ or books, with 107 sub-parvans and 2,111 chapters in all, including the appendix Harivaṁśa. This just gives an idea of the immensity of this epic poem, which is eight times as big as Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey put together.
Since the text contains quite a few riddles known as kūṭaślokas and vast portions of didactic material, several commentators have tried their skill on it. The gloss of नीलकण्ठ (14th cent.) is more well-known and is widely referred to.
Analysis of the Contents
The contents of the eighteen major books may be briefly summarized as follows: Ādiparva, the first book, is fairly long and deals with several ancient episodes connected with शुक्राचार्य, the preceptor of the असुरस्, and his intractable daughter Devayānī, and ययाति, a prominent king of the lunar dynasty, as also the famous romance of शकुन्तला and the king दुष्यन्त. However, the major part of the book is devoted to the story of the ancestors of the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas like Śantanu, भीष्म, Vicitra-vīrya, धृतराष्ट्र and पाण्डु; the birth and एदुचतिओन् of Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas; their early rivalries; मर्रिअगे of द्रौपदी, the Pāñcāla princess, to the Pāṇḍavas; अर्जुन’s पिल्ग्रिमगे and मर्रिअगे with सुभद्रा, sister of Śrī कृष्ण.
Sabhāparva, the second, deals mainly with the performance of the राजसूय sacrifice by युधिष्ठिर, the eldest of the Pāṇḍava princes, the game of dice manoeuvred by the wily दुर्योधन, the eldest of the Kauravas, and its tragic consequences for the former.
Araṇyaparva, also called Vanaparva (and sometimes as Āraṇyakaparva) is the third book that covers the story of the Pāṇḍavas in exile in the Kāmyaka forest. This voluminous book is replete with several stories from the past like those of नल and दमयन्ती, सावित्री and सत्यवान्, of sages like ऋष्यशृङ्ग, अगस्त्य and मार्कण्डेय, as also of kings like भगीरथ and शिबि. The famous quiz, Yakṣapraśna, belongs to this book.
Virāṭaparva, the fourth, is one of the smaller books dealing mainly with the stay of the Pāṇḍavas incognito in the kingdom of विराट. Slaying of the villain कीचक and the battle for rescuing the cattle of the king विराट which had been captured by the Kauravas to force the Pāṇḍavas to come out of their hiding, as also the wedding of the विराट princess उत्तरा with अभिमन्यु, अर्जुन’s son, are the chief incidents portrayed here.
Udyogaparva, the fifth, is also a short book which deals with the peace parleys and preparations for the war, curiously going together. The most touching scene of कुन्ती, the मोथेर् of the Pāṇḍavas, disclosing to कर्ण the secret of his birth in her womb, and the statesmanship of Śrī कृष्ण, who makes a last minute bid for peace, are the highlights of this section. The famous discourse of the sage Sanatsujāta to the blind king धृतराष्ट्र, well-known as the Sanatsujātīya, which is full of philosophical truths, forms a part of this book.
The next book, Bhīṣmaparva, contains the crown-gem of the epic, viz., the Bhagavadgītā. Detailed descriptions of the first ten days of the war containing the superhuman exploits of the grandsire भीष्म, ultimately ending in his being mortally wounded by अर्जुन, form the bulk of this section. Since भीष्म had the unique boon of dying at will, he preferred to lie down on the bed of arrows and postpone his demise till the beginning of उत्तरायण or the northern solstice.
Droṇaparva, the seventh, apart from describing the heroic exploits of Droṇa, the preceptor, culminating in his death through stratagem, also contains an account of the brilliant achievements of the boy-hero अभिमन्यु on the battlefield and his tragic death.
The eighth book, Karṇaparva, details the gory death of the evil genius दुश्शासन, the second of the Kaurava brothers, at the hands of the colossal भीम, and the fall of कर्ण himself at the hands of अर्जुन after a bitter fight.
Śalyaparva, the ninth book, describes the final encounter between भीम and दुर्योधन on the last day of the war, the latter succumbing to the mortal blow received during the duel.
Sauptikaparva, the tenth, delineates the gruesome massacre of the Pāṇḍava army and its allies, in the night during sleep, by अश्वत्थामन्, Droṇa’s vengeful son.
The next book, Strīparva, describes graphically the pitiful lamentations of the women and the widows of the dead warriors.
Then come the twelfth and the thirteenth books, the Śāntiparva and the Ānuśāsanikaparva, containing wonderful discourses on all aspects of धर्म by the patriarch भीष्म at the request of Yudhi-ṣṭhira. भीष्म’s demise and युधिष्ठिर’s चोरोनतिओन् are the other incidents dealt with. The two well-known hymns, Viṣṇu-sahasranāma and Śivasahasranāma, as also the Anugītā (a subsidiary discourse by Śrī कृष्ण to अर्जुन) are parts of these books.
Āśvamedhikaparva, the fourteenth, describes the departure of Śrī कृष्ण for द्वारका and the horse-sacrifice (Aśva-medha) performed by युधिष्ठिर. The humiliation of युधिष्ठिर by a talking weasel that describes the supreme sacrifice of a ब्राह्मण family is an interesting sidelight of this book.
The next book, Āśramavāsikaparva, describes the departure of the old Dhṛta-rāṣṭra to the forest along with गान्धारी, his spouse, and कुन्ती and their subsequent death in a forest fire.
The sixteenth book, Mausalaparva, gives an account of the mutual destruction of the Yādava heroes as also the death of Śrī कृष्ण at the hands of a hunter. The Mahāprasthānika and the Svargā-rohaṇa Parvas, the last two books, give an account of the final journey of the Pāṇḍavas, their death on the way, with युधिष्ठिर alone reaching हेअवेन्.
Characters
The Mahābhārata presents us with a veritable array of human characters, from the sublime to the ridiculous. No type of human emotion, no deed of valour, generosity, sacrifice or meanness is missed here. Nor is there any artificiality in these portrayals. A brief delineation of some of the more important characters may now be attempted here.
Śrī कृष्ण is undoubtedly the most brilliant and picturesque personality projected by the epic. He appears on the scene rather suddenly at the time of द्रौपदी’s स्वयṁवर (formal selection of husband by a maiden princess), and continues to saunter the scenes right up to the end. All his energies are channelized only in one direction: protection of the right and the good, and punishment or destruction of the wicked. His remarkable prowess, matched only by the bewitching beauty of his perfect form, sage counsels, superb stratagems and immensely superior statesmanship, captivate our heart. There is absolutely no doubt that the epic projects him as God Himself come down to save mankind, as he himself admits in the Bhagavadgītā.
Bhīṣma, the grand old man, is another towering personality that awes and inspires us, whether in the supreme sacrifice of abdicating his right to the throne or the vow of celibacy or the matchless heroism on the battlefield. It is but meet that Śrī कृष्ण, who recognized his encyclopaedic knowledge and wisdom, has got it preserved for the posterity by prodding him through युधिष्ठिर to unfold it. The Śānti and the Ānuśāsanika Parvas are practically the repositories of his teachings.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, is perhaps the most dominant character of the epic, next only to Śrī कृष्ण. He was not only a great hero on the battlefield, true to his name (yudhi = in battle, sthira = one who is steady), but a veritable इन्चर्नतिओन् of धर्म or righteousness, a rare combination indeed. That is why he is often addressed as धर्मराज (‘the monarch of righteousness’) too. Come what may, he would never swerve from the path of ethical uprightness about which his thinking was always crystal clear. The Yakṣapraśna-episode is replete with the gems of his wisdom.
The epic pictures भीम, the colossus and अर्जुन, the warrior, in more human terms. If down-to-earth common sense characterizes भीम, अर्जुन is more idea-listic and dreamy. However, both were extraordinarily devoted to Śrī कृष्ण and implicitly obedient to युधिष्ठिर.
Droṇa, the preceptor-warrior who was forced to take to the military profession in spite of being a ब्राह्मण, appears a shade darker than भीष्म. Notwithstanding his learning and austerity, he exhibited a streak of vengeful nature.
Vidura, the son of the maid-servant, is another personality who strikes us not only by his sagacity but also by his intense devotion to Śrī कृष्ण about whose divinity he had absolutely no doubt. Here is a living example to show that it is not birth or caste that makes for greatness but intrinsic character. His discourse to धृतराष्ट्र in the Udyogaparva is now well-known as Viduranīti.
Duryodhana, the eldest of the Kauravas, is the chief villain of the epic. His greed and jealousy overshadowed whatever heroism or virtues he had, resulting in the near-total destruction of the two races and untold misery to millions.
If the word ‘tragedy’ needs any illustration, one should turn to कर्ण. A victim of circumstances, his story can never be read with the eyes dry or the heart unmoved. He was supremely noble and generous in every inch of his personality. He is perhaps the last word for friendship, loyalty and generosity.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the blind and vacillating king, was blind not only physically but also in wisdom. His inordinate infatuation for his children, the Kauravas, prevented him from exercising his authority to uphold धर्म.
Among the women characters it is द्रौपदी, the Pāñcāla princess and the queen of the Pāṇḍavas, that strikes us most. Endowed with striking beauty, a sharp intellect and a sharper tongue which she could wield effectively, she remained absolutely faithful to her husbands. By her supreme sacrifices she has set an example of wifely virtues.
Kuntī, the मोथेर् of the Pāṇḍavas, impresses us as a helpless but noble princess. The fortitude with which she silently bore all her misfortunes and miseries is unparalleled.
Gāndhārī, who made the utmost sacrifice of denying herself the pleasures of eyesight because धृतराष्ट्र, her husband, was born blind, is a paragon of the ideal of wifehood. Unlike her husband, she was bold enough to admonish her son दुर्योधन for his wicked behaviour and warn him of its dire consequences, because she was ever devoted to धर्म.
Veritable Encyclopaedia of Dharma
The Mahābhārata, also known as the Pañcama Veda (‘the fifth Veda’), is a veritable encyclopaedia of Hindu religion and culture. The claim of the सूत Ugraśravas that ‘anything anywhere is an echo of what is here’ and ‘what is not here is nowhere’ is no exaggeration. Every aspect of dharma—whether it is rāja-धर्म (statecraft), आपद्-धर्म (conduct permissible during dire calamities), दान-धर्म (liberality) or मोक्ष-धर्म (conduct pertaining to emancipation)—finds its due place here. In fact, the very purpose of the Mahābhārata is to expound धर्म in all its ramifications. The celebrated Bhagavadgītā, the less known Anugītā, as also the two well-known hymns Viṣṇu-sahasranāma and Śivasahasranāma, have been sources of inspiration to philosophers and votaries of religious pursuits over the millennia. The cult of विष्णु and the reconciliation of the various warring faiths also find an appropriate place. Along with the growth of rigidity of the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम्, honest attempts at extolling human excellence and treating it as the real basis of brāhmaṇahood are also conspicuous. In spite of the misogynists of the age, women did find a place of honour during the epic period.
Mahābhārata Outside India
There is enough evidence to admit that the Mahābhārata had migrated outside India too, especially to the South-East Asian countries. Incidents from this epic have been portrayed in stone relief in the Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom of Kampuchia.
Epilogue
Whether the Mahābhārata was the composition of a single poet or the compilation of several editors, whether the great war was fought in 3100 B. C. or 1400 B. C. or 950 B. C., whether it was a family feud or a ferocious war, it is verily the biggest classic ever composed by man and will retain its relevance as long as the sun and the मोओन् shine or the स्तर्स् twinkle, because it mirrors the eternal drama of human existence.

mahābhiṣeka
(‘the great sprinkling [during the चोरोनतिओन् of a king]’)
------------------------------------------
The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (38) describes the चोरोनतिओन् of इन्द्र as the king of the gods in हेअवेन्. This rite has been called ‘Aindrī महाभिषेक’.
Probably following this, the चोरोनतिओन् of a great king, which includes the sprinkling of water from various sacred sources (= अभिषेक), came to be known as ‘mahābhiṣeka’.
Here are the names of some of the great kings who underwent the महाभिषेक ceremony: जनमेजय, Tura Kāvaṣeya, च्यवन भार्गव, अम्बरीष, and भरत (son of दुष्यन्त).
See also ABHIṢECANĪYA and ABHIṢEKA.

mahālayaśrāddha
(‘śrāddha [performed on the] festival day of [the पितृस् or manes]’)
------------------------------------------
Performance of śrāddhas to appease the dead ancestors is an integral part of Hindu rituals. Out of these, the महालय-śrāddha is a well-known rite. It is to be performed during the kṛṣṇapakṣa or the dark half of the month of Bhādrapada (September), when the sun is in the Kanyālagna (Virgo). It is supposed to give great joy to the manes. It can be performed for the benefit of not only the paternal and maternal ancestors but also for other relatives.
The procedure is almost identical with that of पार्वणश्राद्ध. See ŚRĀDDHA for details.

mahāprasthāna
(‘the great or final departure’)
------------------------------------------
The seventeenth book of the Mahā-bhārata is known as Mahāprasthānikaparva. It describes the final journey of the five Pāṇḍavas along with द्रौपदी towards हेअवेन्.
‘Mahāprasthāna’ means walking continuously towards the north, the Himā-layas, without ड़ोओद् and rest, until the body falls and dies out of sheer exhaustion.
This kind of religious सुइचिदे was permitted to the Vānaprasthins who had completed all their duties in life and found no more reason to live.
It was also prescribed as a punishment for people who had committed heinous sins like murder of a ब्राह्मण or of a foetus, incest etc. However, it was prohibited in the कलियुग. Epigraphical evidences show that certain kings like Gāṅgeya committed religious सुइचिदे which might have included महाप्रस्थान also.

Mahāśivarātrivrata
------------------------------------------
The deity रुद्र-शिव is as old as the Ṛgveda. The शिव cult and शैविस्म् are of hoary antiquity. Hence religious observances on the days considered dear to शिव, must have been existing since the ancient days.
The 14th day of the dark half of every month—kṛṣṇa caturdaśī—is called ‘Śivarātri’ or ‘Māsaśivarātri’. The one in the month of Māgha (February—March) is christened ‘Mahāśivarātri’, since it is the greatest of all.
In several पुराणस् like the Skānda, Padma and Garuḍa, there are stories and passages of hyperbolic eulogy of this महाशिवरात्रिव्रत. One of the common stories is how a निषाद or a किरात (a hunter or an aborigine) who ‘observed’ the vrata on the Mahāśivarātri day unknowingly, out of the force of circumstances, by ड़स्तिन्ग्, keeping vigil and bathing a शिवलिङ्ग (the emblem of शिव) with water, was taken to the world of शिव. How much more would the benefit be, if it is observed knowingly, with devotion!—This seems to be the burden of such stories.
Of all the major Hindu festivals, Mahāśivarātri is the only one wherein the austerity part (as signified by the very word ‘vrata’) is predominant. There is practically no festivity, revelry or gaiety in its observance, the whole thing being one of continuous solemnity. This is but natural since शिव is the god of the अस्चेतिच्स्, the very इन्चर्नतिओन् of वैराग्य or renunciation!
About the origin of Mahāśivarātri, there are several myths. When ब्रह्मा (the fourfaced god of च्रेअतिओन्) and विष्णु were disputing each other’s greatness to establish their own supremacy, a huge लिङ्ग or pillar of fire appeared suddenly between them and a voice from the void declared that he who would find the extremities of this लिङ्ग would be considered the greater one. Neither of them succeeded and were hence obliged to accept the greatness of शिव who had manifested as that pillar of light. This was the origin of शिवलिङ्ग and Mahāśivarātri.
According to the second myth, Mahā-शिवरात्रि is the day on which शिव महादेव, drank the हालाहल poison that emerged out of the milky ocean (kṣīra-sāgara) when it was being churned by the देवस् and the दानवस् (gods and demons), and thus saved the worlds from destruction. A third myth attributes its greatness to its being the day of मर्रिअगे of शिव with पार्वती, the daughter of the mountain king Himālaya. A fourth myth describes this day as the day on which Lord शिव, out of joy, burst forth into a great dance which has since been known as Śivatāṇḍavanṛtya.
This vrata is open to all human beings. The basic disciplines to be kept up on this day are: अहिṁसा (non-injury), सत्य (speaking the truth), ब्रह्मचर्य (continence), दया (compassion), kṣamā (forgiveness) and anasūyatā (absence of jealousy). ड़स्तिन्ग् is one of the most essential aspects of this vrata. So also jāgaraṇa or keeping vigil in the night. Worship of शिव throughout the night, bathing the शिवलिङ्ग with pañcāmṛta (five tasty things—milk, curds, ghee, sugar and honey), होम, जप of the mūlamantra (basic मन्त्र, viz., oṁ namaśśivāya) and prayer for forgiveness—are the other items involved in its observance. He can then, at the end of the vrata, do pāraṇā (breaking the fast by partaking of the offerings).
One may take a vow to observe this vrata for 24 or 14 or 12 years. At the end of this period one has to perform the उद्यापन, a concluding rite indicating the completion of the vow.
In the modern days, ड़स्तिन्ग्, visiting शिव temples and keeping awake in the night are common, though पूजा throughout the night at homes is confined to the more orthodox sections.
The festival is celebrated with great solemnity and éclat in the famous temples of शिव at वाराणसी (Banaras), रामेश्वरम्, चिदम्बरम्, Somanāth, Bhuvaneśvar, Kāḷahasti and other pilgrim centres.

Mahāvīra
(‘the great hero’)
------------------------------------------
See HANUMĀN.
It is also the name of वर्धमान महावीर, the last of the Jaina Tīrthaṅ-karas. See VARDHAMĀNA-MAHĀVĪRA for details.

mahāhavis
(‘the great offering’)
------------------------------------------
Cāturmāsya is the technical term used to indicate three वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् of the इष्टि type—Vaiśvadeva, वरुण-praghāsa and Sākamedha—performed at four monthly intervals. (See CĀTURMĀSYA for details.)
Sākamedha, the last, is spread over two days. महाहविस् or the great offering is an important ritual in this sacrifice. Eight oblations are offered to eight deities like इन्द्र, अग्नि, महेन्द्र and Viśva-karman. Of these eight, five are common to the other two sacrifices also. The other three are cake offered to इन्द्र and अग्नि on twelve kapālas (potsherds), चरु (porridge) to इन्द्र and another cake to Viśvakarman.
See also IṢṬI.

mahāyajñas
(‘great sacrifices’)
------------------------------------------
See PAÑCA-MAHĀYAJÑAS.

Mahānyāsa
(‘the great placing [of the deities on one’s limbs]’)
------------------------------------------
Rudra or शिव, along with विष्णु or नारायण, is a primary deity of the Hindu pantheon. He is said to be fond of अभिषेक or ceremonial bathing. Rudrābhiṣeka or ceremonial bathing of the शिवलिङ्ग by the process of महान्यास is an extremely important part of Śivapūjā or worship of शिव.
According to the tradition set up by बौधायन (circa 600 B. C.) one who wants to worship रुद्र must himself feel his identity with रुद्र first and then only start the worship. The ritualistic process by which this is done is महान्यास. Here the arcaka or the worshipper establishes the various limbs (nyas = to keep or establish) of रुद्र or शिव in his own body as also those of his parivāradevatas (attendant gods) to feel fully identified with शिव himself.
The महान्यास involves a very long process of ritualistic worship of शिव comprising 49 steps! Only a few of these steps, the more important ones, may be briefly dealt with here.
The whole process starts with the usual preliminaries involved in पूजा or ritualistic worship like आचमन (ceremonial sipping of water) and सङ्कल्प (religious resolve) stating the intention as also the procedure to be adopted. This is then followed by several nyāsas like pañcamukhanyāsa wherein the several aspects of रुद्र-शिव are invoked into one’s own body by the worshipper. The next steps are daśāṅga and ṣoḍaśāṅga raudrīkaraṇa wherein रुद्र-शिव is invoked to be established in one’s limbs like the forehead, ears, eyes and face.
Then comes the षडङ्गन्यास involving the six limbs like the heart, the head and the tuft of hair to the accompaniment of Vedic mantras like the Puruṣasūkta.
After inviting शिव for worship, the various उपचारस् (modes of direct service) like आसन (seat), pādya (water for washing the feet) and अर्घ्य (water for washing the hands) are offered.
This is followed by स्नान (bathing) with various items like scented water, भस्म or holy ash, waters in which gold, रुद्राक्ष beads (Elaeocarpus ganitrus) and dūrva grass (Cynodon dactylon) are immersed followed by Malāpakarṣaṇa-स्नान (bathing to remove impurities).
Now follows the most important part of the ritual—rudrābhiṣeka—bathing the शिवलिङ्ग with pure water to the accompaniment of all the mantras of the Rudrapraśna (or Rudra or Namaka) and the Camaka. It is absolutely necessary that the flow of water over the लिङ्ग is continuous and uniform.
Then, the following Vedic sūktas and mantras have to be chanted: Puruṣasūkta; Śrīsūkta; Sadyojāta—mantras of the Mahānārāyaṇopaniṣad; the Daśaśānti and the Ghoṣaśānti mantras.
Other items of पूजा that are performed now are: offering of cloth, बिल्व leaves, rice-grains with sesame seeds, garland of रुद्राक्ष, some specified flowers, incense, lighted lamp and ड़ोओद्.
The whole ritual closes with प्रदक्षिण (circumambulation) and नमस्कार (obeisance).
The tīrtha (holy water) and prasāda (consecrated ड़ोओद्) are then distributed among the devotees.

Mahiṣāsura
(‘the buffalo-demon’)
------------------------------------------
See DEVĪMĀHĀTMYA.

Mahātala
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् describe the universe as comprising 14 worlds, 7 being above this भूलोक or earth and 6 being below it. These six are generally given the name Pātālalokas. However, महातल is the fourth nether world starting with अतल, just below this earth.
It is supposed to be inhabited by multiheaded serpents, all descendants of the sage कश्यप and his wife कद्रू. Some of the chief ones among them are: Kahaka, तक्षक, Suṣeṇa and Kāliya.
Though they are terrible in appearance and cruel by nature, they live in eternal fear of गरुड, the great eagle-mount of Lord विष्णु, an inveterate enemy of theirs.

mahādāna
(‘the great gift’)
------------------------------------------
Dāna or giving gifts has been extolled greatly in the Hindu scriptures, especially in the धर्मशास्त्रस् and the पुराणस्. That this is an important aspect of धर्म (righteous living) in this कलियुग or Iron Age, has also been stressed much.
Out of the several dānas mentioned there, ‘mahādāna’ or ‘a great gift’ is also one. The mahādānas may be ten (vide Agnipurāṇa 209.23, 24) or sixteen (vide Matsyapurāṇa 274 to 289). Some of them are: तुलापुरुष (weighing a person against gold or silver, and distributing it to worthy persons), gosahasra (a thousand milch-cows), horses, elephants, chariots, land, होउसे, bride and servant-maids.
An elaborate and complicated procedure has been set out for making these gifts.
See also DĀNA.

mahāyoga
(‘The great [or final] योग’)
------------------------------------------
In certain aspects of शैविस्म् (vide Vāyavīya Saṁhitā 7.2.37), five kinds of योग are described. Out of these महायोग is the last and the highest. In this state, union with शिव is experienced wherein all other kinds of attractions and attachments are transcended.
The various steps of योग described by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) are generally accepted here also.

Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
The उपनिषद्स् are the last part of the Vedas—hence the appellation ‘Vedānta’ (anta = end)—and contain the quintessence of the spiritual wisdom of the same. This wisdom helps us to loosen our bonds of सṁसार (transmigratory existence), destroys our इग्नोरन्चे of our real nature as the ātman—the pure spirit beyond the body-मिन्द् complex—and leads us to God, giving us the supremely blissful experience.
If the ten उपनिषद्स् upon which शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) has commented upon are considered as the major ones, the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad comes in the series as only next to them. It is the tenth prapāṭhaka or section of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, the earlier three prapāṭhakas (7th to 9th) forming the well-known Taittirīya Upaniṣad.
This work is also known as the Yājñikī Upaniṣad.
There are two recensions or versions of this Upaniṣad known as the Drāviḍa-pāṭha and the Āndhrapāṭha. The former has 64 sections while the latter—the longer version—has 80 sections.
Both Bhaṭṭabhāskara (A. D.1188) and सायण (14th century A. D.) have written commentaries on the shorter version. They have considered this Upaniṣad as ‘khila’ or a supplementary part of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. The longer version also has a commentary but the author’s name is not known.
Another commentary in the name of one Puruṣottamānanda Tīrtha is also available. It is in the kārikā form (in anuṣṭubh verses). The text is either short or incomplete.
Unlike as in the other उपनिषद्स्, the subject matter here does not seem to follow any systematic arrangement or pattern. All the three major subjects of the वेदस्, viz., कर्म (rituals), upāsanā (meditation) and ज्ञान (knowledge) find a place here. Many of the mantras used in the सन्ध्या ritual, pūjās (ritualistic worship) or other rites are found here. Hence it may be considered more as a miscellany of all the subjects left over.
The vast contents may be briefly summarised as follows: description of ब्रह्मन् in his various aspects as प्रजापति, परमेश्वर and अक्षर-ब्रह्मन्; realisation of ब्रह्मन् in one’s heart; knowledge of God alone leads to मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्; God pervades the universe; God is one’s all-in-all; various गायत्री-mantras for upāsanā; prayers to मोथेर् Earth; on इन्द्र; destruction of sins; hymn to दुर्गा; prayers for the attainment of knowledge; prayers for the increase of retentive faculty; good and bad works; God can be seen only by his grace; sacrifices help in getting purity of मिन्द्; नारायण as the cosmic being who also resides in the heart; mantras for consecrating the शिवलिङ्ग; salutation to the various aspects of शिव; on प्रणव; on गायत्री मन्त्र; Trisuparṇa mantras; Madhumantras; prayers for longevity and safety as also wealth; longing for लिबेरतिओन्; विरजाहोम-mantras; प्राणाग्निहोत्र ritual; unity of शिव and विष्णु; truthfulness as the supreme means for लिबेरतिओन्; importance of अग्निहोत्र sacrifices; importance of सṁन्यास; यज्ञ as a potent weapon; description of ātmayajña which is the same as सṁन्यास and saṁnyāsin’s life.
This Upaniṣad is a mine of special information and instructions. The well-known sūktas—the Nārāyaṇasūkta, the Medhāsūkta, and the Durgāsūkta—find a place as a part of the text. Mantras and procedures connected with the सन्ध्या ritual, repetition of गायत्री-मन्त्र, mantras used in the विरजाहोम (a part of the procedure for taking सṁन्यास), the Trisuparṇa mantras (also used in the same), the usual teachings of the उपनिषद्स् connected with आत्मन्/Brahman, मुक्ति, the paths of देवयान and पितृयान as also many principles of philosophy and एथिच्स् are described here in an elegant language.
On the whole it is a very interesting and attractive Upaniṣad, extremely popular in the ritualistic circles.
See also UPANIṢADS.

Mahendra
------------------------------------------
It is one of the names of इन्द्र, the king of the gods in हेअवेन्. (See INDRA.) It is also the name of a famous parvata or mountain, mentioned in the epics and the पुराणस्. It is one of the seven Kulaparvatas or mountains making the boundaries of the जम्बूद्वीप, the island on which Bhāratadeśa (India) is situated. Ten rivers like the Tribhāgā, the Acalā, the ताम्रपर्णी and the Vimalā take birth here.
Paraśurāma spent his last days here. युधिष्ठिर, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas had visited it while on a पिल्ग्रिमगे.

mahāsāntapana
(‘the great [expiation] that burns’)
------------------------------------------
The topic of sins and their expiation (prāyaścittas) has been widely discussed in the धर्मशास्त्रस् as also the पुराणस्. सान्तपन, महासान्तपन and अतिसान्तपन are one variety of these expiations.
See SĀNTAPANA for details.

Mahādeva
(‘the Great God’)
------------------------------------------
Mahādeva is one of the several names and aspects of शिव. He is included among the eight forms (‘mūrtyaṣṭaka’) of शिव or the eleven forms of रुद्र (‘ekādaśarudra’). He may be blue or white in complexion. He is shown seated on a lotus seat with four arms, two holding टङ्क (hammer) and kṛṣṇamṛga (deer), the other two showing abhaya and varada mudrās. He of course, has threes eyes and his hair is arranged as जटामुकुट, crown of matted hair or he may have the usual crown also.

Mahīdhara
------------------------------------------
It is very difficult to understand the वेदस्, not only because of their archaic language but also because they are closely associated with a system of rituals with which we are not at all familiar.
Out of the several commentators on the वेदस्, महीधर also is one. He might have lived in the 16th century and probably composed his commentary, the Vedadīpa on the Mādhyandina Saṁhitā of the Śukla Yajurveda around A. D. 1587.
Mahīdhara was a resident of काशी. In his commentary he has been influenced by Uvaṭācārya (11th century A. D.) an earlier commentator on the same work, to a great extent. However, his explanations are more detailed. He quotes profusely from the श्रौतसूत्रस्.
He has another work also to his credit, the Mantramahodadhi, a work on the तन्त्रस्.

Mahābhāṣya
(‘the Great Commentary’)
------------------------------------------
The Aṣṭādhyāyī of पाणिनि (5th century B. C.) has been considered as a unique and unparallelled work of Sanskrit grammar—or for that matter, any grammar of any language—by well-known scholars of Sanskrit as also Indology.
As the very name indicates, it is a work in aṣṭa or eight, adhyāyas or chapters. It has 3996 sūtras or aphorisms in all.
The Mahābhāṣya is a commentary on the Aṣṭādhyāyī, by पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.). It covers only 1228 sūtras. It is written in a simple conversational style. It throws much light on contemporary life and culture.
Whether this पतञ्जलि is the same as the author of Pātañjala Yogasūtras has been hotly debated. However, Hindu tradition considers the two to be identical.

Mahāvākyopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor उपनिषद्स् and is assigned to the Atharvaveda. There are only twelve mantras, mostly in prose. Parts of this Upaniṣad are identical with the Puruṣasūkta and the Nārāyaṇopaniṣad.
The fourfaced ब्रह्मा, the creator, is the teacher here. Having found a worthy disciple, he starts teaching this secret and sacred knowledge to him, advising him to give it only to the pure सोउल्, introvert in nature and who pleases the teacher by devoted service.
There are two types of people in this world: those who consider this world to be real and those who know that it is not real. The former, entertaining desires and ambitions, take to the pravṛttimārga, the path of वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् and get into bondage. The latter, endowed with the eye of wisdom, take to the निवृत्तिमार्ग or the path of renunciation, seek मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्, realise ब्रह्मन् and become free even here and now.
This आत्मन् (inside) which is the same as ब्रह्मन्, is not darkness but brilliant light. This is realised by the repetition of the Haṁsamantra (haṁsaḥ so’ham) by identifying the spirit in the sun with one’s own Self.
This realisation of the most brilliant आत्मन्/Brahman cannot be compared to समाधि (perfect concentration), योग-siddhi (perfection in योग) or manolaya (dissolution of the मिन्द्). It is actually an experience of oneness with ब्रह्मन्.
Verses 8 to 10 are identical with the verses 16 to 18 of the Puruṣasūkta and describe the God-vision of the perfected sage.
The eleventh verse describes the identity of the light of the sun and the light of the आत्मन् inside brought about through meditation with प्रणव or Om.
The last section (12th मन्त्र or verse) gives the phalaśruti, the benefits and results of studying this Upaniṣad, which is the same as the total destruction of sins and dissolution into Lord विष्णु.

mahājanapadas
(‘great countries’)
------------------------------------------
Janapada or rāṣṭra is a country and its people. Certain janapadas seem to have acquired the name ‘mahājanapada’ during the period of early बुद्धिस्म्. They were sixteen and were spread over the Indo-Gangetic plains. Though they were small territories, they might have got this appellation either due to the greatness of the dynasties of the kings that ruled them or because they were prosperous and militarily strong.
Some of them are: अङ्ग, Magadha, काशी, कोसल, Vajji, कुरु, Pāñcāla, Śūra-sena, काम्भोज, Avantī and गान्धार.

Mahāmāyā
(‘the [goddess of] great delusion’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the names of दुर्गा since she is unlimited creative energy and delusive power (mahā = great, māyā = creative energy or delusive power). She is often identified with Viṣṇumāyā (vide Bhagavadgītā 7.14), the special power of विष्णु responsible for च्रेअतिओन्, preservation and destruction.
The मार्कण्डेयपुराण (85.34) describes her as a secondary manifestation of Mahākālī, the tāmasik aspect of Mahā-लक्ष्मी.
She is generally described as a goddess of the complexion of red hibiscus flower, having three eyes and four arms carrying ikṣukodaṇḍa (bow of sugarcane), puṣpabāṇa (arrow of flowers), पाश (noose) and raktotpala (red lotus).
The goddess associated with Amara-nātha शिव (in the cave of Amarnāth, Kashmir) is also called महामाया. This is one of the शक्तिपीठस् where the neck of सती-दाक्षायणी is supposed to have fallen.

mahatpariṇāma
(‘transformation [that gives the aṇus or atoms] mahattva or practical dimension’)
------------------------------------------
The वैशेषिक दर्शन is one of the six recognised systems of Hindu philosophy. It has developed its own atomic theory of च्रेअतिओन्.
Out of the seven fundamental basic principles of च्रेअतिओन्, the four elements—earth, water, light or fire and air—are in the form of paramāṇus or extremely minute atoms. They have existence but no perceptible dimension.
However, when by the will of ईश्वर or God and the totality of the karmas of the unredeemed souls of the previous च्रेअतिओन्, the process of च्रेअतिओन् starts, two paramāṇus—of course, of the same element like the earth—join together forming a द्व्यणुक or a diad. When three such dvyaṇukas join together forming a tryaṇuka then only it attains mahattva (perceptible dimension) and dīrghatva (length and breadth). This change in the paramāṇus becoming ‘mahat,’ is called ‘mahatpariṇāma’.
See also VAIŚEṢIKA DARŚANA.

mahāvedi
(‘the great altar’)
------------------------------------------
Somayāgas—Vedic sacrifices wherein the oblation of the सोम juice is the most important rite—need a lot of space, time and preparation. A special वेदि (altar or platform) has to be constructed for performing them. This altar is called ‘mahāvedi’.
It is laid out to the east of the usual place of the गार्हपत्य and आहवनीय fires. It is a trapezium measuring 36 steps east to west, 30 (or 33) steps north to south on the west and 24 steps north to south on the east. The area is marked by driving pegs on the ground at the appropriate places.
It contains many places specially marked or reserved for various priests and objects used in the sacrifice.

Māhiṣmatī
------------------------------------------
The city of माहिष्मती (now identified with the ओङ्कार-Māndhātā island in the river नर्मदा, 64 kms. or 40 miles from the modern city of Indore in Madhya Pradesh) has been mentioned not only in the epics but also in the पुराणस्. It was the capital of the powerful king Kārta-vīryārjuna who had once humbled the mighty रावण (the king of लङ्का) himself. The sage परशुराम attacked and killed कार्तवीर्यार्जुन at माहिष्मती later on.
It was also the capital of Daśāśva, a son of the famous king इक्ष्वाकु.
Sahadeva, the last of the Pāṇḍava heroes, is said to have conquered the king Nīla who was reigning at माहिष्मती at that time.

mahābhāva
(‘the great emotion’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term especially used by the Bengal school of वैष्णविस्म् nourished by श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य (A. D. 1485-1533) and his disciples as also his followers.
An ordinary भाव or emotion, is the joy derived from enjoying the worldly objects. When the object is God Himself and the intensity of joy reaches such a height that the devotee feels himself as one with God, it is termed ‘mahābhāva’. The gopis of Vṛndāvana are normally given as the ideal example for this state. श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य also is believed to have experienced this state quite often.

mahābhāgavata
(‘a great devotee of God’)
------------------------------------------
The Pāñcarātra Āgamas (texts devoted to the worship of विष्णु) speak of a devotee of God as a ‘mahābhāgavata’ (‘a great devotee of God’) if he has the following qualifications:
He must have undergone the five purificatory rites known as pañca-सṁस्कारस् like ब्रन्दिन्ग् on the arm.
He must be practising nine modes of भक्ति like smaraṇa (remembering the Lord), कीर्तन (singing devotional songs), arcana (worship of God) and so on.
He must have a thorough know-ledge of the five doctrines (arthapañcaka) like the true nature of God, the सोउल्, means to मोक्ष and other items.
See ARTHAPAÑCAKA and PAÑCA-SAṀSKĀRAS.

mahāśānti
(‘the great propitiatory rite’)
------------------------------------------
When problems, troubles and difficulties arise which are beyond human efforts and capacities to get redemption from, human beings are apt to take to religious or divine remedies. शान्तिस् or propitiating rites belong to this class. महाशान्ति is one such rite prescribed in some ancient works like the Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhyasūtras (5.11).
Mahāśānti is performed when mishaps such as the following occur or for general well-being: fall of meteors, before the चोरोनतिओन् of a king or before he starts on an invasion, birth of a baby under an inauspicious star, falling down of holy objects like the umbrella of a deity in procession, when costly things are lost, during eclipses and so on.
It is generally done on a specially raised platform wherein there will be an agnikuṇḍa (fire place) as also places for kalaśas to be established. Mostly Ṛgvedic mantras are recited during the ceremonies. A होम also is performed. The yajamāna (main performer) takes a bath at the end. The śāntijala (holy water used in the rite) is sprinkled over him by the priests who are then suitably rewarded.
See also ŚĀNTIS.

Mahālakṣmī
------------------------------------------
There are two aspects of महालक्ष्मी. The first is the same as लक्ष्मी, the consort of विष्णु. (See LAKṢMĪ for details.)
In the second aspect, as depicted in the Devīmāhātmya or Durgāsaptaśatī, she is the same as दुर्गा or पार्वती, who destroyed the demon महिषासुर. She is described as light red in complexion and seated on a lotus. She has eighteen arms holding various weapons like battle-axe, mace, bow and arrow and lance as also other items like lotus, rosary, wine-cup, conch and bell.
In the annexure to the same work known as Prādhānikarahasya, she is depicted as the first to appear (before everything) and the other deities like ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and महेश्वर, as also their consorts, to have emanated out of her.
The cult of महालक्ष्मी is essentially शाक्त in orientation.
The most famous temple dedicated to her is at कोल्हापुर् (also known as Karavīrakṣetra) in Maharashtra.
See also KOLHĀPUR.

mahānāmnī
(‘of great fame’)
------------------------------------------
It is the name of a group of nine verses of the Sāmaveda (Jaiminīya Saṁhitā 2.7) beginning with the words ‘vidā maghavan’. These verses are also called Śakvarī verses. They are chanted on various occasions as during अहीन sacrifices.
They are chanted as a part of वेदव्रतस् (religious rites connected with the commencing of Vedic studies) and also as expiation for certain kinds of sins.

mahālaya
(‘the great dissolution’)
------------------------------------------
In the works dealing with हठयोग, the word ‘mahālaya’ or लययोग is used in the sense of समाधि (highest superconscious experience) wherein the जीव or the individual सोउल् loses his identity in शिव or परमात्मन् (the Supreme Self) even as a drop of water gets merged in the sea or salt gets dissolved in water.
The sādhana of लययोग has nine parts. See LAYAYOGA for details.
The word महालय also represents महालय अमावास्या occuring in September-October, when the पितृपक्ष (the fortnight considered as extremely auspicious for performing obsequial rites to the departed ancestors) comes to a close. It also indicates the commencement of the Dasara festival from the next day.

mahāvākyas
(‘great sentences’)
------------------------------------------
The post-शङ्कर writers on Advaita Vedānta have mentioned four sentences, taken from four उपनिषद्स् and belonging to the four वेदस्, which teach the unity of the आत्मन् and ब्रह्मन्, as four ‘mahāvākyas’ or great sentences. They are: prajñānam brahma (‘Consciousness is ब्रह्मन्’) from the Aitareya Upaniṣad (5.3) of the Ṛgveda; aham brahmāsmi (‘I am ब्रह्मन्’) from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad of the Yajurveda (1.4.10); tat tvam asi (‘You are That’) from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.8.7) of the Sāmaveda and ayamātmā brahma (‘This आत्मन् is ब्रह्मन्’) from the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad (2) of the Atharvaveda.
